Flight-tracking analysis · Nov. 13, 2026

Empty skies

Departures from U.S. airports stopped almost all at once at 12:38 p.m. Pacific, 16 minutes before the FAA's nationwide ground stop officially took effect. Then the sky slowly emptied.

Just after 12:38 p.m. Pacific time on Friday, the steady stream of departures from American airports stopped. For the half hour before, about 36 airline flights took off every minute, much like the same hour a day earlier. Within two minutes, the rate had dropped to a handful, and it stayed there: 6 a minute on average over the following half hour. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop, which the agency attributed to a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control, took effect at 2:54 p.m. Central (12:54 p.m. Pacific), according to News9. Public flight-tracking data shows the departures stopped 16 minutes before that. Nothing new was going up. The flights already in the air carried on to their destinations, and the number of aircraft over the country fell steadily, from 6,552 at the moment of the collapse to 878 at 3:59 p.m. Pacific. A day earlier at the same time, 5,751 aircraft were airborne.

The cliff came first

Counting airline takeoffs minute by minute makes the timing plain. The rate did not taper off as you might expect if airlines were holding flights at the gate one by one. It fell off a cliff, from the high 30s per minute to single digits, between 12:38 p.m. and 12:40 p.m.. The official ground-stop time comes 16 minutes later, in the shaded gap below. Early reports cited the 2:54 p.m. Central time. The data suggests departures were already being held in practice before the formal nationwide order. One possibility is that facilities hit by the communications outage stopped releasing flights on their own first. We could not find an official FAA timeline that settles it.

Everywhere at once

The halt did not roll across the country as a wave. Splitting departures into rough time-zone bands, the same test finds the collapse at 12:36 p.m. in the East, 12:39 p.m. in the Central band, 12:40 p.m. in the Mountain band and 12:38 p.m. in the West (all Pacific time), within a few minutes of each other. At the biggest hubs, the half hour after the cliff looked like an airport closed for the night.

data.text/html:
Two states kept flying

Alaska Airlines said in a statement that flights within Alaska and inter-island flights in Hawaii were not affected by the ground stop, The New York Times reported. The tracking data agrees. After 12:38 p.m., airline departures in Alaska ran at 95% of the previous day's level for the same hours and Hawaii at 89%. In the lower 48 states the figure was 7%. Hawaiian Airlines' Boeing 717s kept shuttling between the islands, and international flights by Japan Airlines, ANA, Korean Air, Qantas and Philippine Airlines kept leaving Honolulu. In Alaska, Alaska Airlines' in-state jets, regional carriers such as Bering Air and Ravn, and the cargo flights that stop in Anchorage kept flying.

The neighbors stopped flying to the U.S.

The FAA controls only U.S. airspace, but the stop reached across both borders. Canadian airports suspended U.S.-bound flights while domestic Canadian flights carried on, Global News reported. And the FAA asked Mexico's federal aviation agency to keep all aircraft at Mexican airports with scheduled flights to the United States on the ground, the Mexican agency said, according to The New York Times. The data shows the same split. Departures from Canadian airports that went on to enter U.S. airspace fell from about 28 per half hour to 6, while flights that stayed out of the U.S. ran at 99% of the previous day's level. Mexico points the same way, with far fewer flights in the data: U.S.-bound departures went from 6 to 1 per half hour, and other flights ran at 100% of normal. The volunteer receivers that feed this data cover far less of Mexico than of the U.S. and Canada, so the Mexican numbers are small.

data.text/html:
Watch the sky empty

Every aircraft broadcasting its position over the U.S., one frame per minute. Press play, or drag the slider back to late morning to see an ordinary Friday. Aircraft are colored by altitude; grey ones are on the ground with transponders on. Canadian and Mexican traffic is shown faded. Hover over a plane for its callsign and type.

Landings kept coming

Takeoffs and landings normally track each other closely. That's how the number of aircraft aloft stays roughly level through the afternoon. After 12:38 p.m. the two lines split: takeoffs dropped to near zero, while landings continued at close to their usual pace as flights already en route reached their destinations. The gap between the lines is the sky draining.

The middle of the sky emptied first

Sorting airborne aircraft by altitude shows the order the sky emptied in. The layers between 15,000 and 35,000 feet, where jets climb out after takeoff, thinned fastest because nothing new was climbing through them. Two layers held up longer: cruise altitudes above 35,000 feet, where long flights already en route kept going, and the lowest band under 5,000 feet, which is mostly small private planes and helicopters.

Who is still flying

Airline traffic fell furthest, and the mix of what remains aloft shows it. At 3:59 p.m. Pacific, compared with the same time a day earlier, airborne traffic by category stood at: helicopter 40%, general aviation 23%, other 20%, airline 11%, business jet 6%. Helicopters (police, medical, news) and small private planes make up a growing share of what is still flying.

Data

Positions come from adsb.lol, an open, unfiltered network of volunteer ADS-B receivers. It publishes a snapshot of every aircraft it hears every 10 seconds, in one file per half hour, usually 30 to 60 minutes after the half hour ends. This page downloads those files when it runs and keeps one position per aircraft per minute. Each position is assigned to the U.S., Canada or Mexico using Natural Earth borders, extended about 100 km offshore. "Over the U.S." includes Alaska and Hawaii. The page compares Nov. 13 with the same clock hours on Nov. 12. Aircraft types come from the tar1090 aircraft database.

Definitions

Takeoff: an aircraft's track goes from on the ground to airborne, or a track first appears in the air below 2,500 feet. Airline: an airline-style callsign (three-letter operator code plus flight number) or a medium or heavy jet. This includes regional and cargo carriers, and a few flight schools that use operator codes. Collapse time: the first minute after 11 a.m. Pacific when airline takeoffs over the next three minutes average less than 40% of the preceding half hour's rate. The same test is applied to each region. Into U.S. airspace: a departure from Canada or Mexico whose aircraft appears over the U.S. within four hours. This also catches some Canadian domestic routes that cut across U.S. airspace. Coverage of Mexico is much thinner than of the U.S. and Canada.

Caveats

Receiver coverage is incomplete, especially at low altitudes and in remote areas, so absolute counts are undercounts. The comparisons (before vs after, Nov. 13 vs Nov. 12) are more reliable than the totals. The 2:54 p.m. Central ground-stop time is as reported by News9; other outlets give only "Friday afternoon", and we could not find an official FAA timeline.
